fact: HISP Ethiopia and the HISP Centre state that in November 2025 UNICEF partnered with them to give the Ministry of Education and regional education bureaus technical assistance on DHIS2-Ed, working directly with schools, woreda education offices and zonal education departments in the SER, SWEPR, Oromia and Benishangul Gumuz regions.

HISP states that the DHIS2-Ed project works directly with schools in four regions (SER, SWEPR, Oromia, Benishangul Gumuz) and lists developing tools to collect learning outcomes and student attendance as an activity still to be done; it gives no number of schools and calls the work neither a pilot nor a rollout.

HISP describes the national platform as the Ministry of Education's national EMIS enterprise application, with UNICEF, the HISP Centre at the University of Oslo and HISP Ethiopia providing technical assistance to the Ministry and regional education bureaus.

The DHIS2 education implementation page states that the Government of Norway and UNICEF provide the financial backing for the Ethiopia DHIS2 education work begun in November 2025; it names no domestic funding.

The DHIS2 page states that a partnership between UNICEF and the HISP Centre at the University of Oslo was initiated in November 2025, working with schools, woreda education offices and zonal education departments in four regions (SER, SWEPR, Oromia, Benishangul Gumuz).

UNICEF, the grant agent, reports that by June 2025 the digitisation of EMIS had been finalised and piloted, with no count of pilot schools given; deployment to 4,500 primary schools in 156 weredas, with 4,500 computers, was planned for July 2025 to June 2026 and had not begun.

The Ministry of Education developed and completed the web-based EMIS and finalised an EMIS Directive for it, with World Bank support; the system gives unique identification numbers to students, teachers and schools and covers federal, regional, woreda and school levels.

The platform was developed under a GPE System Capacity Grant through the World Bank, its school computers and training are paid from the GPE STEP grant through UNICEF, and US$15,062,600 of the grant's top-up is tied to EMIS digitisation; no domestic budget line is stated.

In the year to 29 June 2025 the real-time digitised EMIS was fully developed, tested and piloted, 1,322 EMIS and planning experts (132 women) were trained, and the tender for 4,500 primary-school computers was set for August 2025.

The Ministry of Education's ESDP VI gives a baseline of 'None' both for a student database and for a system using digital technology for school information and data on pupils' daily schooling, and 0 for institutions networked for EMIS; the plan gives no date for these baselines, so the publication year 2021 is used.

fact: UNHCR was piloting its Digital Education Platform in late 2019, registering each child in refugee camp schools by registration card every semester, with rollout to all camps expected in early 2020; it covers refugee camp schools only and no count of schools is given.

Under UNHCR's Digital Education Platform each child is registered in the database once a semester by reading a registration card at the school or camp, linked to the refugee registration profile; the study describes this as at late 2019, in refugee camps only.

The Digital Education Platform is UNHCR's, with dashboards to be opened to the Government and partners through a portal under procedures still to be set, and its relation to the ministry's EMIS not yet clarified, as at late 2019.
